title: Spatial Visualisation and 2D/3D Shapes
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Spatial Visualisation and 2D/3D Shapes. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Representing solids

A three-dimensional object can be described by its faces, edges and vertices. A net is a flat arrangement that folds along edges into a solid without overlap. Orthographic views show the object from a chosen direction; perspective drawings suggest depth.

Visualising transformations

Rotation changes orientation but preserves shape and size. A reflection produces a mirror image. When mentally rotating a labelled solid, track one distinctive face or vertex rather than relying on a visual impression.

Cube reasoning

In a cube net, adjacent faces share an edge after folding; opposite faces do not share an edge. If a cube is painted on the outside and cut into equal small cubes, the number of painted faces depends on whether a small cube is at a corner, edge, face interior or fully interior.

Worked example: A cube painted on all six faces is cut into (\(n^3\)) unit cubes. For (\(n \ge 2\)), corner cubes have 3 painted faces, non-corner edge cubes 2, face-interior cubes 1, and interior cubes 0.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Mark a reference face before folding or rotating a diagram mentally.
  • For painted-cube counts, classify by location instead of listing every small cube.
  • Use the net's shared edges to infer adjacency; page proximity alone is not enough.
  • Check the stated viewing direction before comparing front, side and top views.
  • Rotate the object mentally while keeping labels attached to the same face.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
  • For an (n by n by n) painted cube: corners = 8; edge-interior cubes = (\(12(n-2)\)); face-interior cubes = (\(6(n-2)^2\)); inner cubes = (\((n-2)^3\)), for (\(n \ge 2\)).
  • A net must have exactly six square faces and fold without overlap.
  • Rigid rotations and reflections preserve all lengths and angles.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    How many vertices does a cube have?

    1. (\(6\))
    2. (\(8\))
    3. (\(10\))
    4. (\(12\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(8\))

    A cube has four vertices on each of two parallel square faces: (\(4+4=8\)).

  2. Core:

    A triangular prism has 5 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have?

    1. (\(8\))
    2. (\(9\))
    3. (\(10\))
    4. (\(11\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(9\))

    Use (\(F-E+V=2\)): (\(5-E+6=2\)), so (\(E=9\)).

  3. Foundation:

    How many faces does a cube have?

    1. (\(4\))
    2. (\(6\))
    3. (\(8\))
    4. (\(12\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(6\))

    A cube has six square faces.

  4. Standard:

    A cube is painted on every outer face and cut into (\(3^3\)) equal cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?

    1. (\(8\))
    2. (\(12\))
    3. (\(18\))
    4. (\(24\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(12\))

    Each of the 12 edges has (\(3-2=1\)) non-corner cube. Total: 12.

  5. Challenge:

    A fully painted cube is divided into (\(4^3\)) unit cubes. How many small cubes have no paint?

    1. (\(4\))
    2. (\(8\))
    3. (\(16\))
    4. (\(27\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(8\))

    Only interior cubes have no paint. Their count is (\((4-2)^3=8\)).
